utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom and also to the videolink courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I do understand that there are a few preliminary matters to be dealt with first before we start the videolink and before we invite the witness to be escorted into that videolink room. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We have actually two short preliminary matters. First is that we anticipate that tomorrow we might need a bit more time with the witness who should finish his videolink tomorrow, so it could be that we'll need maybe half an hour longer than usually. And the second is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour in addition to what, exactly? Going beyond quarter past 2.00, or half an hour beyond what you had estimated?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, going beyond quarter past 2.00. I'm not asking for any additional except this hour I already asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we'll see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I'll try to cut it down also to be -- only I have to introduce four documents with this witness at the beginning as non-associated exhibits, that's why I'm cautious and ask for a bit more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. That's for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to go beyond quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how about Mr. Mladic's presence? And --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic waives his right to be present tomorrow. He has visit and he -- that's the second preliminary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say that's for the whole of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We also could consider if Mr. Mladic is not present to start at 9.00 and then to -- because I have to, of course, to check with everyone whether no agendas are filled after quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can inform you that the Defence does not have any problem with starting at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's just have a look. We'll consider then half an hour extra tomorrow, still to be decided whether we start at 9.00 or whether we go beyond quarter past 2.00. If the Prosecution is already in a position to give its views on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We would have no problem with either schedule, and like Mr. Lukic I'll attempt to be efficient tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let me see. Then, of course, it needs some organisation which is primarily in the hands of Madam Registrar. We'll hear from her soon after she has consulted the interested parties, and I'll consult with my colleagues as well. Any other matter, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not for now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there was an issue to be raised by the Prosecution as well. But if it's not urgent, we could also leave it to a later point in time. I see that the Prosecution would save it for -- as you say, save it for a rainy day, but ... Then let's just check whether the videolink is functioning well. Madam Registrar at the far end of our videolink, can you hear us, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours. I hereby confirm that we can see you and we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the sound quality is such that -- although not perfect, still workable. Could you tell us who is present in the videolink room?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, apart from myself there is a ICTY technical support officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Technical support officer. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must see that I've seen videolink images which were better, but -- and the sound is not the best I've heard in my life, but I invite the parties to intervene whenever they think that the quality falls below acceptable stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the microphone is switched off at your end, Madam Registrar, but perhaps that's for escorting the witness into the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. I'm also addressing the interpreters' booth, whether the quality is sufficient to work with? And I get a signal that it is not. Therefore, could we get the assistance necessary. And it may that be while the witness is standing that he's too far off from the microphone, so could we do another test. Madam Registrar, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is a delay in the sound. There's a delay in the sound. There's overlapping of syllables.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please sit down, Madam Registrar, so that we have more or less the same situation as if the witness is speaking while being seated. Could you again?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour. Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think that the quality is not good enough. I get a signal from our interpreters that we should not work on this basis. Perhaps it is a matter of reinstating the connection because it seems that it's not a local problem but rather a relay problem. I suggest that we'll break off the existing communication, try to re-establish it, because the same is true, by the way, for the images.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes. Not always. I suggest that the videolink will be ended and that it will be restarted again. We take a break of five minutes for that purpose. We'll resume at ten minutes to 10.00. --- Break taken at 9.43 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see on my screen that the microphone is switched off at the other side of the videolink. Madam Registrar, could you switch it -- it's on now again. Can he hear us? Can you see us? And this is a question both to Madam Registrar and to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour. We can hear you and we can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I put on the record that it is still not a perfect link, and I invite both the booth and the parties to address me when they consider that they cannot work on the basis of the quality we have at this moment. Witness, I just remind you that the -- you've given a solemn declaration that was given by you, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. That was received and interpreted. So we'll now start your examination. You'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please slowly state your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Tomislav Delic. Father's name Gojko.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones in the courtroom please be switched off, thank you, when the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have on our screens 1D1729, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Delic, there's a document on the screen before you. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this page, do you see a signature and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us look at the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see the signature there? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, at one moment -- actually, on two occasions did you give a statement to the members of General Mladic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. Did I give what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A statement.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I gave the statement that is here, with that signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to look at the statement; and what is written in the statement, is it recorded correctly?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and it's correct. However, there are some minor points, probably typing errors, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there something that you'd like to correct in this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I have nothing to change in this signed statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you said and what is written in this statement, is it correct and true?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you give me the same answers?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I'd give the same answers, but I don't know if the word order would be the same. I mean -- but the answer would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections by the Prosecution. Therefore, Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1729 receives number D929.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D929 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will not have any questions for this witness. I'll just read the statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, Tomislav will testify about the establishment of political parties in the area of Sanski Most. He will also explain the situation in the municipality immediately before the war. Mr. Delic will explain his role in the efforts to calm down the situation. Despite these efforts, the very next day the Muslim active and reserve police launched an armed attack and seized the municipal building. It was then that Serbs realised that Muslims and the SDA did not care about peace. Mr. Delic will explain the process of disarming and his role in this process. His battalion took part in the disarming of Muslims in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje no earlier than the third day of the fighting. He claims that none of the members of his battalion committed any crimes. He thinks that misdeeds were done by people who were not from the area of Sanski Most. In Mahala, he saw individuals from Banja Luka looting the deserted Muslim houses. Those were criminals who put on the SOS uniforms. Mr. Delic will explain the situation close to the end of the war when Arkan's Tigers arrived in his municipality. Mr. Delic will explain the impact of World War II genocide against the Serbs on the events in Sanski Most municipality in the 1990s and that there were -- was not a part of the territory of Krajina in which the Ustasha did not commit crimes against the Serbs. It was the fear that their neighbours would murder them mercilessly again that contributed most to the unity of the Serbs in this area. Their unity was not influenced by any individual or organisation but by the fear of carnage and their wish to remain in this area. They were united by Jasenovac as the largest execution site for the Serbs and by the other mass graves from World War II. Mr. Delic will testify about his knowledge regarding the incidents alleged in the indictment. That was statement summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Jeremy, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. You'll soon see him on your screen. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 3 of your statement you refer to your involvement in the establishment of the SDS in Sanski Most. You refer to a conversation that you had with President Karadzic at the founding meeting of the SDS in Sanski Most. Now, this conversation took place in September 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, skipping forward in your statement to paragraph 18 where you talk about a conflict that you were involved in with your battalion. You say that you were with your battalion in the fight for the liberation of Jajce. This was in October 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly switch off all unnecessary microphones, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you say that you were wounded during this time and you spent a year outside of your unit. You spent this year in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, there's a part of your statement that's -- is entitled "The Impact of the World War II Genocide Against the Serbs on the Events in Sanski Most Municipality in the 1990s," and that's -- that's 11 paragraphs of the 36 that appear in your statement. Now in the paragraph that follows that section, paragraph 33, you discuss the killing of approximately 28 men at the Vrhpolje bridge on or about the 31st of May, 1992. Now, you state: "I am sure it was an act of revenge," and you suggest the reason for this revenge was the killing of 300 Serbs in Kljevci village, 51 years earlier. Now, is your conclusion that these events were motivated by revenge based on an assumption that you have made, or is it based on information that you -- that you got from the perpetrators of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I concluded this based on my line of thinking. I was aware of what happened in 1945 in Kljevci and Vrhpolje. My predecessors told me. There was a grave and a monument. It now is gone. It has been demolished. What happened, happened, and that's the only inference I could make as a human being. I don't know what else to conclude. I don't know who did it. I was not present when those things were done, but I heard that they had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I'd like to switch topic and to the topic of the SOS or the Serb Defence forces whom you discuss at various points in your statement, paragraphs 15, 16, and 21. Now, you say that the purpose of the SOS was primarily the psychological protection of the Serb population, and that's paragraph 21. Now, Mr. Delic, you knew some members of the SOS forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you a document in connection with these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31868.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, in front of you, you should see a document issued by the Serb Defence Forces staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most. It's dated the 13th of April, 1992. And we see that it is a proclamation. Now, focusing on the first paragraph of that proclamation, we read that it's informing the Serb people and the general public of the Serb municipality of Sanski Most that a unit of the Serb Defence Forces, SOS, was formed on the 12th of April, 1992, in Lusci Palanka. And we read how it is capable of protecting the Serb people of the territory of the Serb municipality of Sanski Most in a given moment as well as protecting all others whose security comes into jeopardy. So what we read there in that first paragraph is consistent with what you say in your statement about the SOS protecting the Serb people in Sanski Most; yes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, moving down a couple of paragraphs, we read that: "On the 12th of April, 1992, following a decision on the forming of the unit, it was inspected and linked up with other units, according to the principal of the territory and the requests of the military strategy." Now, sir, there's evidence in this case that the SOS was involved in the mopping up operations in Mahala, Hrustovo, and Vrhpolje. Now, you -- you were also involved in these operations as a member of the 6th Brigade in late May and early June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the 4th Battalion which held the positions on the so-called Greda, near Poljaci and Sehovaci and Sasina. That was the line. I was not in town. I don't know what was happening there. I was not present in town. As for the first combat activities, I was on that axis that I just described. I can state that not a single bullet was ever fired from that line towards Sehovci, Poljak, and Sasina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But just to be clear, you yourself took part in the disarming of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the third day of those activities. I would like to highlight that, day three.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at the end of this proclamation we read that: "All commanders of sections and commanders of units are invited to come to their designated places within 24 hours of this proclamation being publicly announced and to take further instructions for their work." And it's signed the Serb Defence Forces. Now, Mr. Delic, at least in the early part of May 1992, you were a member of the SOS; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Somebody inscribed me, just informally. I never participated in any of their actions, but I knew some 15 lads from the day they were born, so to say. But I never participated with them in any of the actions. I don't know who inscribed my name there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to look at an exhibit in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Before I do, I'd like to tender this document, 65 ter 31868.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 31868 receives number P7202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7202 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please see P3294 on our screens. And could we please go to page 33 in the English and 26 in the B/C/S. And this is the -- this is the diary of Nedjeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is the diary of Nedjeljko Rasula whom you discuss in your statement in paragraphs 3 and 4, for example. Focusing your attention on the bottom of the page on the right-hand side of the B/C/S original version, we see that there is a Crisis Staff meeting, and it's dated the 6th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to the next page in each language. And if we can focus on the left-hand side of the page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, in front of you, you should see a list of names, number 1 to 33, and at the top of that list, we see the heading SOS. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we see 33 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we skip forward one page, please, in English. Sorry, could we go to page -- it should be page 34 in the English. 35 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We just had it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So we see the list of 33 names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, at 33, in the English, I see a different name from that of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think the witness is -- I'm going come to it, but I think the witness's name is at number 30 in -- in each list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, sir, we see at the top of this list, number 1, Dusan Saovic. Now he was the commander of the SOS; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And it's -- it's been mentioned, but we see your name at number 30, Tomo Delic, father's name, Gojko. That's a reference to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that should be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So we see that according to Nedjeljko Rasula, on the 6th of May, 1992, you were one of the 33 members of the SOS. Now at this time, May 1992, Nedjeljko Rasula was president of the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, there is also testimony in this case that -- that you were a member of the SOS, and that testimony is from Grgo Stojic. And that's at transcript page T4105. Now, sir, Grgo Stojic was the only surviving victim of an attack near Skrljevita village on 2nd of November, 1992. You recognise the name; yes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you discussed this incident in paragraph 36 of your statement. And just so that we are clear, this is the incident where a number of Croats were returning from the market on the 2nd of November, 1992, and they were intercepted by four armed Serbs who questioned them and then executed at least seven of them. Now, that's the incident that you're referring to in paragraph 36 of your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Listen, this is how it was. What happened in Skrljevita, that has nothing whatsoever to do with the SOS. Individuals did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, yes, we --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: That had nothing to do -- there was a suspect who was brought in and who was put on trial. And as for the SOS, none of them were from the SOS. There was one Dani Kajtez, who --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, we'll have an opportunity to go through this --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- step by step.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: That incident had nothing to do with the SOS. But it wasn't an incident. For me, it was a murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: As I say, sir, we'll go through that step by step. But I think it's -- it's clear that we're referring to the same incident. Now, there's evidence in this case --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- at transcript page 4075 that the victims of this incident were from Skrljevita and Kruhari. Now, Kruhari is to the immediate west of Skrljevita; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you're from Kruhari; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the very beginning of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you were the SDS representative for Kruhari, on the local board; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: At that time and -- that I'm -- it was Ratko Ninic because I was already a soldier of the 5th Battalion. I represented my local commune politically, but it was Ratko Ninic who actually represented it formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But while you were an SDS representative, you were living in Kruhari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now in his testimony in this case, T4070 to 4071, Grgo Stojic stated that before the executions began, each of the victims were asked about the whereabouts of an Ilija Tutic and a Bono Tutic. These men are known to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Ilija Tutic? Is that the name you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned two names: Ilija Tutic and Bono Tutic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I know Bono Tutic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: He's a Croat. He is a Croat, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir, Grgo Stojic in -- on the same page as I've referred to testified about a meeting that you held with Bono Tutic about -- on the subject of disarming in the village of Skrljevita. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now you say in your statement, and you've mentioned again today, that you heard that these killings were committed by Danilusko Kajtez, and this Chamber has indeed received evidence that --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this Chamber has received evidence that Danilusko Kajtez was, indeed, one of the four perpetrators in this incident. And that's transcript page 4070 to 4071. Now, Mr. Delic, Danilusko Kajtez was also from Kruhari; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had moved to Kruhari with his parents. You know, the natives of Kruhari are very special people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So you knew him personally; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I did. I knew him from the day he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement, and you've again said today, that Danilusko Kajtez was detained and punished for the Skrljevita events, and in your statement you say he was in prison in Banja Luka. Now --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that he was punished. I said that he was on trial and that he was detained in Banja Luka. I don't know whether he was punished or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, did you have an opportunity to review your statement before you swore to the truth of its contents today?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Where was I supposed to review it and see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, you were asked --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked today if you had had an opportunity to review your statement before you swore to the truth of its contents.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, I did review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if I can focus your attention on paragraph 36 of that statement, and that's where you talk about the events that we're talking about now in respect of Skrljevita and Danilusko Kajtez. Do you have that paragraph in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, we see that it states as follows: "As regards the killing in Skrljevita, I heard they had been committed by Danilusko Kajtez who was detained and punished for that." So, sir, in fact, you did say in your statement that you know that Danilusko Kajtez was punished; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they are two words: Sanctioned and punished. In my view, when I uses the word "sanction" and when I interpret it, that means that he was brought in to prevent him from perpetrating other crimes. Now when you say "punish," that means that he is serving a prison sentence. That's how I see it in my mind, and this is a difference in the way I would put it and I would express myself with this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Lukic, you are speaking both languages. Would you like to have the translation verified, whether the word "sanction" was used or the word "punished" was used?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the statement I can see "sanction" in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In B/C/S. So therefore, perhaps it's -- well, first of all, Mr. Lukic, if that is of any importance, you should have looked at it. But apart from that we, of course, want to have the most accurate interpretation. I don't know who made it but perhaps if would be good to have it verified, especially on this word.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And I think I can just -- if I could ask one more question just before the break on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not saying that you shouldn't continue, but I just notice that there is a -- that there may be a language issue. Please proceed. Apart from, of course, whether the word "sanction" means what the witness says it means. That's a different matter. But nevertheless, to start such a discussion should always be done on the basis of the most accurate interpretation and then that could be the starting point for further discussion on the meaning of those words. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this Chamber has received evidence that even in December 2000, despite previously spending some time in custody, in prison, the Banja Luka District Court was still looking for Danilusko Kajtez who had not been tried for the Skrljevita events. That's P3556. Now my question, sir, is that you're not aware of any sanctioning or -- formal sanctioning or formal punishment of Danilusko Kajtez prior to December 2000, are you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: No. You mean for this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes. So, sir, I think your answer is no; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm moving to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, we'll continue. Mr. Jeremy will put further questions to you. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, now, you say in your -- and staying on this topic of Danilusko Kajtez and Skrljevita. You say in your statement that you are certain that Kajtez was not a member of any unit at that time, at the -- at the time of the events in Skrljevita. Now, by "unit," you're referring to a military unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I mean a military unit and I mean the SOS. He was part of the SOS, but to the best of my knowledge, and the late commander Dusko used to say that, he'd say Danilusko is the worst one I got. He took some weapons and went I don't know where. So he got a weapon, walked around, and he knows what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you say that he was a member of the SOS. And referring to the document that we were looking at before, P3294, which is hopefully still on our screens --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to P3294, please. And if we could go to page 34 in the English and page 27 in the B/C/S, please. If we can focus on the left-hand side of the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And so we see in this list, number 18, a reference to a Dane Kajtez, father's name Gojko. That's a reference to Danilusko Kajtez, the man we've been discussing today; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, so we agree that he was a member of the SOS at a certain time. Now, this Chamber has also received evidence that Kajtez was a member of the 6th Brigade during the war period, and that evidence is P2420, which is a document from the Banja Luka Military Court which released Kajtez back to his unit shortly after these events in -- and the release was in early 1993. Now, sir, not only was Kajtez a member of the 6th Brigade but he was actually also in the same battalion as you, the 4th Battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, Danilusko Kajtez is a man who I think is sick. Now when I think of it all, I think he is a sick man.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: He was registered here --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: -- but not in a single operation. He did not take part in a single operation of the 4th Battalion. You can get the exact answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- from the battalion commander, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please answer the question. The question was whether Danilusko Kajtez actually was also in the same battalion as you were, the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. He was never at the front line with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Now for the next exhibit I'd like to look at, it's under seal, so could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you say in your statement that your company, the 1st Company of the 4th Infantry Battalion of the 6th Brigade, was comprised of inhabitants of your birth village, and that's in paragraph 6. So, sir, as a member of the 4th Battalion of the 6th Brigade, Danilusko Kajtez would have been in your company; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: He was supposed to be, but he wasn't. If he was in the 6th Sana, he was never with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, you say in your statement in paragraph 36 that in respect to these events in Skrljevita, Kajtez acted completely independently. Now, is this an assumption that you have made or is it based on perhaps a conversation that you had with Danilusko Kajtez?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you saying that it's absolutely an assumption --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, I didn't talk to him about that. And he never told me about any of that. But I did talk -- I mean, when people heard that he had done that, then I did talk to these men from SOS, and they said to me, You know that he broke off from us, that is he a renegade. 4th Battalion? No way. No way. I don't know who he would have gone with in the 4th Battalion. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to put it to you that the reason that you are attempting to distance Kajtez from the VRS, from the SOS, and from yourself and to depict him as a renegade is because you yourself were involved in the ordering of this attack in Skrljevita. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. How can you say that? How can you say that I am disassociating myself, that I'm distancing myself? I'm distancing myself from that man as a person, as a person. I mean, I don't know who can testify that he was in the army. You have the battalion commander. Go ahead and ask him. You have young men who were in SOS. Ask them whether he went into operations with him. He took weapons and he knows what he did. How could I issue orders for Skrljevita?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've answered the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P366 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this is a handwritten letter signed by Danilusko Kajtez. It's sent to Vlado Vrkes. Sir, focusing your attention on the document before you, we read as follows: "Brother Vlado and the rest of you gentlemen." And I'm going to focus on a few paragraphs here. The first one states: "Vlado, my wife came to visit me on Tuesday (19 April) and said that the lawyer Tomic told Neso over the telephone that he couldn't help me." In the next paragraph, we read: "This means that he anticipates a harsh sentence and therefore wants to distance himself in time. "I can't take this endless and painful investigation any longer. You are all supposedly working on my behalf, but in fact nothing is happening and you don't give a damn. You just care for yourselves." Skip the next paragraph. The one after that, we read: "Vlado, you know as well as the rest of you, what and how much I have done for the [sic] damned Sanski Most." Skipping on: "What I'm about to say to you, to all of you, now is a very serious matter and please take it that way, as this is my only way out." Skipping the next paragraph, and if we can -- well, we see at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S: "You know that out of Manjaca ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "... I and a few others liquidated 12 people on two occasions, which was ordered and witnessed by inspector Vujanic Mico Krunic who was the warden of the Betonirka prison at the time, Mile and other inspectors, the chief at that time was Vrucinic." Mr. Delic just stopping there, you're aware of this particular incident; correct? This incident where a number of men suffocated?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Skrljevita, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm focusing --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: What, rather?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you wait until Mr. Jeremy has finished his question and not interrupt him. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, my question is this: We see -- we saw in the text this reference to 12 people being liquidated at Manjaca. And my question to you is: Are you aware that a number of persons suffocated when being transported from Betonirka to Manjaca on the 7th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Delic. It's a question to you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: As regards these people that you mentioned, 12 who suffocated, I don't know anything about that. I don't know about anybody suffocating in Betonirka. I don't know about that, either, because I never even stopped by Betonirka when these bad times started, if I can call them that. I never stopped by. I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's clear, sir. Thank you. Now returning back to this letter that we have before us, I'm going to move forward two further paragraphs where we read as follows: "As for this charge against me, the gist of my defence will be that we went hunting and were attacked. If I get a harsh sentence, in other words, if you fail to get me out of here, I will say that I killed on orders issued by Tomo Delic and Vlado Vrkes with the intention of resettling the village of Skrljevita as soon as possible. All of which could easily be proven in court." Now, sir, that's a reference to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: My name is mentioned but nothing doing. At the beginning of the text, I was following this, he said that he couldn't take it any longer and that he should be helped. Now, who did he mean? He meant Tomo Delic should do something to set him free. Judge, sir, if he knew you, he would address you, too, in order to get out of prison. Because Tomo Delic was an eminent citizen of Sanski Most who had capital and who earned it through his own hard work. Tomo Delic, son of Gojko, real name, Tomislav. Everybody appreciated whatever he said. This, this deserves condemnation. Now he is invoking my name. Since he was my neighbour, he probably thought that Tomo Delic would try to do something. His mother came to see me, "Tomo, try and do something," and also they organised demonstrations, and I told the people to go back home. You cannot allow people to commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Danilusko Kajtez. Danilusko Kajtez, he'd write anything to get out of prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to put it to you that Danilusko Kajtez has not written to you saying, "Please, Tomo Delic, prominent individual in my village, get me out of prison." He has written to say that he will tell people that he has killed on the orders of Tomo Delic. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you can claim whatever you want. What I'm saying is the truth. Many of the allegations that you are making are incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this Chamber has received evidence that shortly after the attack on the Croats on the 2nd of November, 1992, Croats from Skrljevita left for Croatia and this was not only because these men were murdered but also because of subsequent murders, intimidation, and looting of property. And that's the testimony of Grgo Stojic, transcript page 4075. Sir, this Chamber has also received evidence that you, Tomo Delic, exploited the fear created by this attack and that in these circumstances Croats from your village, Kruhari, signed their property over to you and departed Sanski Most. That's the testimony of RM015, transcript page 17312 to 17313. And, sir, that's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: That is not the truth. Do you want an explanation for this entire story?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir, we'll continue to move through this document. Now, I'm going to skip down four paragraphs below the paragraph that we've just been looking at where we read -- and if we can go to page 3 in the B/C/S, halfway down that page 3. We read: "There is still a month or two left before the trial so do something if you can. If you can't, then we'll meet in the dock, behind bars, all together - you, Vrucinic, Vujanic, Krunic, Mima, and Tomo Delic, because - illegible - ordered me to do this. Why should you all be better or greater Serbs than me?"

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the English, please, and if we can go to the final page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, towards the end, before the signature, we read: "That is all this time and for the last time. Your Vojvoda duke," and we see the signature. Below that we see a post-script, which reads as follows: "Go to Talic, Mladic, Karadzic, to whoever you can think of, but get me out of here." And in the very last paragraph, we read: "My fellow prisoners here, from various towns, who also killed the Balija and the Ustasha, are being acquitted and helped by their municipalities. Only Dane is being put into deep shit by his own side. So be it, Serb gentlemen." Now, Mr. Delic, this Chamber has received evidence that Danilusko Kajtez was eventually released from prison on the 14th of March, 1995. That's P372. And, sir, you knew that he was released subsequent to the writing of this letter to, among others, yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: You know what? I heard about this letter after the war. I heard that he had written it. But I knew when he was released from prison. His house was close to mine. He passed by my house and he told me, "Here I am, out of prison." You have to know that I drew my weapon at him because he had attacked a Croat in my courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, you would agree that after this incident in Skrljevita, more Croats did, indeed, leave Sanski Most, and they left Kruhari, and they left Skrljevita. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Almost everybody left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, Witness, I have one question. It was put to you that property of those who had left was signed over to you. Now, did that happen at all? Did you acquire any property which earlier belonged to those who left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is how things transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why did they transpire as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how things transpired. Mr. Milan Martic, the late Milan Martic, has a son, Ivica, who is a parish priest in Sanski Most. In 1941 he saved some members of my family who were taken to be killed in Susnjari, and the same thing happened 50 years later. I had to protect Milan Martic from that Danilusko Kajtez. He cursed my mother. Milan Martic was in my courtyard, and then Danilusko Kajtez said, "I am going to kill both of you." I also had a house on the Island of Krk. Mile told me, "Tomo, I cannot drag you and your family into that." I told him, "Mile these are documents of my house on Krk. Go there and you draw a contract here showing that I was protecting your property here." The only Croatian house in our local commune belongs to Milan Martic. It is still here. His wife is alive. No other house has remained intact but that one because everybody knew that Tomo Delic was protecting it. They returned to their house immediately after the war. Ten days after the BiH army entered Sanski Most, his wife arrived and found in her house all the appliances and everything else save for those things that that had been plundered by BiH soldiers. So this is how things transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have another question. In paragraph 15 of your statement -- and perhaps it can be shown to you. Paragraph 15 is dealing with your battalion taking part in disarming of Muslims. It says at the end: "In Mahala, I saw individuals from Banja Luka looting the deserted Muslim houses. Those were criminals who put on the SOS uniforms." First of all, could you tell us who these persons were? Do you have names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know any names. When I went to see what was going on there, somebody told me that they were from Banja Luka. Because all the criminals from the whole areas plundered under the guise of the SOS. I was watching them being chased from Mahala. So they put on SOS uniforms in order to plunder under disguise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How are you sure that they were not SOS members then if you don't know who they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Dusko Saovic told me that dishonourable acts were committed under the guise of the SOS. They then issued a document asking not to be called the SOS anymore but to be incorporated into the 6th Sana Brigade. The words I heard from them was, "Everybody and their uncle are looting, pretending to be SOS." I know that they stopped being SOS. They became members of the 6th Sana Brigade based on a document. I believe that document still exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, did you know all the SOS members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not all of them. Some 15 lads or so, did I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if the SOS had more than 15 members, you wouldn't know whether those you saw in so uniforms, whether they were members yes or no. You wouldn't know that, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But their commander told me that they were not SOS members. A lot of was happening between the commander of the SOS and Rasula and Vlado. Arguments, quarrel, harsh words. All sorts of commotion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the commander with you in Mahala, the SOS commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I went there to see what had happened you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my question was when you went to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness's words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just let me finish -- well, I repeat my question: When you went there to see what had happened, were you accompanied by the commander of the SOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander took me in his car. He told me, "Let's go there to see what's going on."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were there together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the car. We were in the car. We did not leave the car to take a stroll around. We just drove by. As a citizen, I was curious to see what had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you saw individuals looting. Did he see that as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two of us saw it. And after that, he said: "I'm going straight to Rasula to see what we can do." He told me, "This one's from Banja Luka," "This one's from Prijedor." I didn't know those people. That's why I'm telling you that I saw things. I was with him, I was in his car. He told me that they were not SOS members, and after that he decided to issue that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you go there with the SOS commander who then sees people dressed in SOS uniforms, looting, saying that they are not SOS members, and he didn't get out of his car and he didn't address those saying, Why are you wearing SOS uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He just cursed one who was close to the car. He didn't dare get out because that man had an automatic rifle and the commander only had a pistol. I suppose he knew him. I know he cursed his mother, but he didn't get out of the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was your unit involved in any way in disarming Mahala or attacking Mahala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My unit was on position on Kruhari near the Sana river and also on the Sava riverbank. I don't think that any of the soldiers of the 4th Battalion ever went to Mahala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about what happened in Mahala before this looting started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you say you went --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When before? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you went there to see what had happened and you saw persons looting. Now, was your unit involved in the previous stage; that is, before the looting started, whether there was any disarming of the population of Mahala or whether there was any attack on Mahala village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My unit was not in the territory of Mahala. When I went to visit Mahala, I think it was on day four or five after those night activities and shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your unit was not there. Do you have any knowledge about an attack on Mahala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None of the soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question is whether you have any knowledge about any attack on Mahala or any combat or any disarming that happened before you went there and saw the looting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke to Ostoja Cukovic, who was their battalion commander. He told me that Mahala would be disarmed. We had to be in our positions. I was near Sehovci, Poljaci, and Sasina with my company, and the others were elsewhere. And obviously when the fighting started, I have to tell you it was terrible to listen to the bullets flying from all over the place. And as for Kruhari, Kruhari is somewhat elevated above the Sana valley. So when fire was opened from there, the bullets reached us. So we spent more time on the ground than standing up. I don't know who was shooting at whom. I don't know because I wasn't there. In any case, prior to that, I was told that Mahala would be disarmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Finally, one question, spontaneously when asked whether you had been a member of the SOS, you referred to a list. Had you seen that list before, the list that was later shown to you as a part of the diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw a list. The late commander Dusko told me, "I am going to put your name on my list." And then I said, "Well, the age is not suitable, and I am also a member of the 4th Battalion." He said, "I would do it." I said, "No, no, don't." We met each other when the corridor was being broken, and then I was a member of the 1st Battalion when the action at corridor was taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. But did you know that your name was put on a list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew because one man told me that he received a salary. He -- it was my salary. He told me, "Boss, I took your salary based on the SOS list." I don't know what the salary was. I don't know whether they received any salaries, why he told me that in the first place. But in any case, he told me that he had claimed my salary based on the SOS list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By whom were they paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't even know whether that information was correct or whether he was just pulling my leg. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier told us that you do not know who inscribed your name on the list; whereas, a minute ago you gave me a full explanation of how your name ended up on that list because you said Dusko told you -- would you please -- would you please not interrupt me. A minute ago, you told us that someone announced to you that your name would be put on a list; whereas, earlier you said you have no idea. Any explanation for why you said you don't know who put your name on the list and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a clue that I was there. I had two bars. They came to my bars and he told me, "Boss, I'm going to put your name on the list." But I never knew that that had come through. And then the other one came and said, "Boss, I'm claiming your salary." Again, I don't know whether it was just a rumour, whether somebody was pulling my leg. I thought that those were just rumours, you know, the type of stories you hear in a bar. I never knew that anything was made official, that my name was actually put on any list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not aware of that until today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not officially. Until today, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And unofficially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unofficially -- Tomo Delic was everywhere. Whenever somebody needed money or something else, my name would come up. That goes to show what kind of a person I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. But spontaneously you told us that your name was inscribed on a list. So apparently you had some knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rumours. People came to my bar. They had a drink or two and then they would tell me, "You are our member." Or the other would say, "No, you are our member." Nothing ever came officially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just need to make several clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, further questions will now be put to you by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have P31 -- actually, it was 65 ter 31868. I didn't jot down the exhibit number, if it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So P7202.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Delic, you were shown this document before. Do you see it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a proclamation. It doesn't depict a stamp or a signature. Did you see documents issued by SOS? Did you know if they looked like this? Do you know how they issued their documents?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw any of their documents. I don't even know that they issued any documents. I don't know whether any of their documents would look like that. But now I can see that they did. You say that they did. It says the Serb Defence Forces staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at P3294. It is Nedjeljko Rasula's diary. Just bear with us while the representative of the Registry calls up the document on the screen in Banja Luka. First, you were shown page 33 in English, which is also page 26 in B/C/S. This is about a Crisis Staff meeting. That meeting was supposed to have taken place on the 6th of May, 1992, according to Mr. Rasula's diary. There's no reference to the SOS on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the following pages in both versions. [In English] If we can move to the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was Nedjeljko Rasula's position in the SOS? Did he hold any position?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He was president of the municipality or mayor, the president of the Crisis Staff as well. I don't know what he had to do with the SOS. I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here we can see 33 names on the B/C/S page, and there is the year of birth for every person on the list except for you and Dragan Camber.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Who is that? I haven't a clue. Listen, if I had inscribed my name anywhere, I would have provided my full name, my year of birth, the times whereas they were, so I suppose if you were joining something they should have known your full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I was going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness has interrupted the counsel. The question was not completed so the answer cannot be interpreted either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, wait for a second. Mr. Lukic will repeat his question. Would you wait until that question has been finished and then again answer the question. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Tomo your name or your nickname?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: In business terms, they call me Tomo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us -- we have your answer. I thought that your answer was not recorded but it has been. You mentioned that you gave the key to your house on the Island of Krk to Mile Martic. Just for the record, where is Krk?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: In Croatia. The Island of Krk, off the share of Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the Martic family ever used your house on Krk?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of Mile Martic's wife? And you say that she is still alive.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Slavka Martic. Her son is the parish priest in Sanski Most. His name is Ivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Delic. This is all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot follow here English channel, so I am not following the pace since I cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're not blamed in any way for not being able to do that. Mr. Lukic, I was just about to intervene because what the witness said about the house in Krk was really not in relation to the question I put to him, so therefore it doesn't arise from any of the questions, at least, in the examination. Any further questions, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I had one or two questions arising out of your questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Delic, a few more questions. It's almost done. Listen carefully. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Further cross-examination by Mr. Jeremy:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to go back to this topic of Mahala which you discussed with the Presiding Judge a few minutes ago and which you also discuss in your statement. Now in paragraph 11 of your statement, you -- you refer to the conflict in the settlement of Mahala. Now, that was -- can we agree that was on the 25th or 26th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Is he asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you -- in your statement you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In the statement you say: "Immediately before the conflict in the settlement of Mahala," apparently you have an idea about chronology, and Mr. Jeremy now asks you whether it was on the date he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the date. It was a long time ago. I don't remember the date, but I remember the events. And I am giving you my account of the events as I remember them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Please, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you've spoken about looting after the conflict in Mahala. It's correct that this looting happened after this conflict that you refer to in paragraph 11; correct.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I was there on the fifth or sixth day. The conflict was over, so there was no more conflict going on, and looting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, and that goes to the essence of my question: You were asked today whether your unit was in Mahala before this conflict began, and you said that: When I went to visit Mahala, I think it was on the fourth or the fifth day after the activities and the shooting. Now, I read in paragraph 12 of your statement that you say: "Before this conflict, I went to Mahala with Ostoja Cukovic." So can we agree that you were, in fact, in Mahala before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, I received a telephone call from one of my waiters. He said, "War is starting." I went to the cafe, went to town, and I said, "What's up?" And they said, "The Muslims by the school took weapons and they started attacking us." This was before the conflict. And I said then, "I'm going to Mahala to see," because I thought that I was a citizen who could walk around. Then Ostoja Cukovic said, "I am coming with you." We got into my car and we slowly drove through Mahala. Around the corner, you could see people with weapons who moved out of the way when they saw a car coming up. Then -- I forgot the name of the school in Mahala, but people were there with all kinds of weapons. Hunting weapons, different kinds of weapons. I got out of the car and I addressed people with the following words: "People, can we say 'merhaba' instead of 'pomoz bog,'" and people recognised me there in the dark and said --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, can --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: -- "Tomo, that's you, is it?" And they said, "What's up?" And I said, "I don't know." And then there was this man called Irfan. He had a hunting carbine and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you've answered my question. So in fact --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- you weren't only in Mahala four or five days after the conflict broke out but you were also there before. You've clarified that. I thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one final question. Do you know where you say that the Muslims used heavy weaponry in the events in Mahala, whether, from the Serb side, any artillery or mortars were used, or do you have no knowledge of that at all?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: There was shooting from all sides. Mortars were being fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From both sides?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, both. Falling on the left and right side of town. One was in Serb hands; the other one in Muslim hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were no houses in the town hit by mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were houses that had been hit. Even in my street a house had been hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were houses hit by Serb mortars and by Muslim mortars or by one of them only?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV DELIC
utterances.text: I was not a mortar man, and I did not command a squad of mortars, so I'm not in a position to say anything. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Then, Witness, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the videolink location and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we continue, what is the programme for the remainder of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We understood you yesterday, Your Honour, that you said that we should continue with the witness who testified the previous two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He said, "That's it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's good to have at least additional interpreter. And if it's not contradicted by the booth, I exceptionally will thank you for serving as an interpreter, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It was on the English channel where we speak otherwise, so we cannot use the channel in two ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, if -- I think we should conclude the videolink so that we do not watch the witness any further, not knowing that he is watched.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, we would recall, and my colleague Ivetic would continue with Mr. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that the next videolink witness is available tomorrow and not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's my understanding too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's our understanding as well. We'll take a break first and then we'd like to continue hearing the testimony of Mr. Subotic after the break. We'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for Mr. Subotic to be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I received confirmation from all interested parties that we could sit tomorrow starting at 9.00 and continuing until quarter past 2.00 at its latest. Therefore later when we adjourn, I'll mention a time different from usual. And I take it that all the formalities for the waiver will be completed, if they are not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They are, Your Honour, and sent to Ms. Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Subotic. Mr. Subotic, again, we had to give priority to the videolink as I explained to you earlier. That's inevitable. And we regret that you have to wait for such a long time. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and Ms. Hasan will now continue her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Now, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- you describe escorting the convoy of vehicles from Nova Kasaba to Bratunac, and you led that convoy together with three soldiers in a BOV 7; that's right?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a combat armoured vehicle of the infantry, yes. With four soldiers only, I think. Or three? I cannot remember exactly, but around that figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: These were all members of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment; these were all MPs?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, members of the battalion of the military police that belonged to the protection regiment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And the Praga that was escorting the convoy from the rear, the Praga had also a commander and a number of soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Praga was also from the artillery battalion that belonged to the protection regiment. It was firing support. There was the commander of the crew and three soldiers, I think. I think three.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So is it correct, then, both vehicles were -- belonged to the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just so we're clear about these vehicles, could we look at a very short clip from the Srebrenica trial video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sound relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we can start at the clip at 00:22.04. And we could just play a few seconds of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We can stop it right there. That's at 00:22.08.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, this vehicle that we see in the back, and I'm not claiming that these are the vehicles of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, but is that a BOV 7? Is that the kind of vehicle that was leading the convoy?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that -- I think that this is a BOV 5 or 6. This is a combat vehicle that is meant for anti-aircraft defence. It's similar. I had a machine-gun, and this is an anti-aircraft gun that is mounted on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And the vehicle that we saw in front of this one - and if you'd like, I can replay that - was that a Praga?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if the witness wouldn't like it, I would like to see it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It was very short. In fact, Ms. Stewart, I think, has captured the image right there. That's at 00:22.06.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Is that the kind of vehicle that was at the rear of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not our Praga. It is a type of Praga. We had Jotifka [phoen] Pragas. That is an older Praga type. It is a Praga but it's not from our regiment. We had one that was a bit more modern; that is to say, the modification was better as far as I can see here in this photograph. It's a bit blurred. And background as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, en route -- and we're done with this video. En route to Bratunac, you would have driven past the Sandici meadow and the agricultural warehouse at Kravica. You do know where that warehouse is?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly. I think I know, roughly. There are two or three buildings, something red, white. If that's what I mean? I mean, a red-and-white building. Is that the warehouse? Is that what you mean, actually?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It's on the right-hand side. It's a big agricultural warehouse. It's the only one in that area, so I think we are talking about the same thing. Now, did you hear any shooting or sounds of exploding hand-grenades coming from the direction of the warehouse when you passed by along that road?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC [Resumed]
